\section*{Random MAX-3SAT: an explicit high-density bound and the fixed-density gap}

\subsection{Definitions and mathematical statement}
\paragraph{Shared notation.}Standard number systems are denoted by $\mathbb N,\mathbb Z,\mathbb Q,\mathbb R,\mathbb C$; index ranges, computational models and specialized notation follow the cited problem source and the definitions below.


$n$ is the number of Boolean variables and $m$ the number of random clauses. $A(F)$ counts the clauses satisfied by the algorithm and $\operatorname{OPT}(F)$ the maximum satisfiable count; expectations are over the instance distribution and any algorithmic randomness.

Polynomial time means a number of elementary steps bounded by a polynomial in the encoded input length. A decision problem is in $\mathrm{NP}$ if yes-instances have polynomial-length certificates verifiable in polynomial time; NP-hardness is under polynomial-time reductions.

A $k$-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most $k$ literals; a literal is a variable or its negation. Satisfiability asks whether a Boolean assignment makes every clause true. MAX-SAT instead maximizes the number or weight of satisfied clauses.
\paragraph{Statement recorded in the supplied source.}
For fixed clause size $r$ and density $m/n$, design a polynomial-time algorithm for random MAX $R$-3SAT instances $F$ that returns an assignment with expected value $\mathbb{E}[A(F)]\geq(1-\varepsilon)\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(F)]$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. \href{https://doi.org/10.4171/owr/2004/28}{[S2]}
\paragraph{Scope qualification.}
The supplied name MAX $R$-3SAT and parameter $r$ are retained. The random-clause distribution and relation between these symbols must be read from the report; they are not replaced by a different random-SAT model.
\paragraph{Source status.}
The supplied catalogue labels this record partially solved. Its source-status metadata was checked against the supplied snapshot on 2026-10-11. This import does not independently establish current open status or mathematical correctness. The catalogue literature assessment is dated 2026-08-21.

\subsection{Short English statement}
Find efficient assignments whose expected score approaches the expected best possible score for random satisfiability instances.

\subsection{Sources}
\begin{itemize}
\item[S1] Ulam AI and the UnsolvedMath Contributors, UnsolvedMath: A Curated Collection of Open Mathematics Problems, record 30000057 (OWR-730-006). Catalogue curation and metadata: CC BY 4.0. The supplied source question is retained; definitions and the English summary are editorial additions.
\url{https://huggingface.co/datasets/ulamai/UnsolvedMath}.
\item[S2] Approximation Algorithms for NP-Hard Problems (2005), Oberwolfach Reports, DOI 10.4171/owr/2004/28, pp. 1461--1540
\url{https://doi.org/10.4171/owr/2004/28}.
\item[S3] random MAX-3SAT approximation theorem
\url{https://doi.org/10.1051/ro:2007008}.
\textit{Underlying Oberwolfach Reports material retains its source-specific licence, including CC BY-SA 4.0 where applicable; see THIRD\_PARTY\_NOTICES.md.}
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Verbatim supplied catalogue question}
For fixed clause size $r$ and density $m/n$, design a polynomial-time algorithm for random MAX $R$-3SAT instances $F$ that returns an assignment with expected value $\mathbb{E}[A(F)]\geq(1-\varepsilon)\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}(F)]$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.

\section{Distribution and source scope}
The primary discussion distinguishes approximating the optimum value
from finding an assignment with a ratio guarantee. The cleaned question
asks the stronger assignment guarantee in expectation. Its clause-size
symbol $r$ is not a new parameter silently substituted for the source's
three-literal clauses. We analyze the explicit model in which each
clause independently chooses three uniform literals with replacement
from the $2n$ literals. This makes precise one reading of the source's
random choice; no claim is made for an unspecified different distribution.

\paragraph{A fixed assignment and a bound on the expected optimum.}
Every fixed assignment makes exactly $n$ of the $2n$ literals false.
All three draws are false with probability $1/8$, so the number
$X_a$ of clauses satisfied by assignment $a$ has expectation
$qm$, where $q=7/8$. Different clauses are independent. We claim
\[
qm\le\mathbb E\operatorname{OPT}(F)
\le qm+\sqrt{mn\log2/2}.
\]
The lower bound follows by using any fixed assignment.
For the upper bound, if $B$ is a Bernoulli variable, the function
$h(t)=\log\mathbb E e^{t(B-\mathbb EB)}$ has $h(0)=h'(0)=0$.
Direct differentiation shows that $h''(t)$ is the variance of a
Bernoulli variable with its exponentially tilted success probability,
and is at most $1/4$, since $u(1-u)\le1/4$. Twice integrating
gives $h(t)\le t^2/8$ for $t\ge0$. Independence now gives
$\mathbb E e^{t(X_a-qm)}\le e^{mt^2/8}$. There are $2^n$
assignments, so
\[
\mathbb E e^{t(\operatorname{OPT}-qm)}
\le\sum_a\mathbb E e^{t(X_a-qm)}\le2^n e^{mt^2/8}.
\]
The first inequality holds because a maximum of nonnegative numbers
is bounded by their sum. Jensen's inequality for the exponential
gives $t(\mathbb E\operatorname{OPT}-qm)\le n\log2+mt^2/8$.
Choosing $t=\sqrt{8n\log2/m}$ proves the claim for $m,n>0$;
$m=0$ is immediate. Jensen here also follows from the supporting-line
inequality $e^x\ge e^u(1+x-u)$ with $u=\mathbb EX$.

\paragraph{What this actually proves for an algorithm.}
The deterministic algorithm returning the all-false assignment has
expected score $qm$, though its score on an individual formula need
not be at least $qm$. If $m=cn$, the preceding estimate yields
\[
\frac{\mathbb EA(F)}{\mathbb E\operatorname{OPT}(F)}
\ge\frac{q}{q+\sqrt{\log2/(2c)}}
\ge1-\frac{1}{q}\sqrt{\frac{\log2}{2c}}.
\]
The last inequality is $1/(1+x)\ge1-x$ for $x\ge0$,
obtained by multiplying by $1+x$. Thus a density
$c\ge\log2/(2q^2\varepsilon^2)$ suffices for the requested
expectation ratio in this specified model. This is an elementary
high-density observation, not a scheme for every fixed density and
arbitrarily small $\varepsilon$.

\paragraph{The failed extension to a fixed sparse density.}
For fixed $c$, our error bound divided by $m$ is a positive constant,
not a quantity tending to zero with $n$. The union over $2^n$
assignments contributes the $n\log2$ term that survives after
optimization. A concentration statement for $\operatorname{OPT}/n$
around its unknown expectation cannot remove this term or compute
that expectation: it locates the random value around an unspecified
center. This is the exact point where combining a trivial assignment
with concentration fails to prove a PTAS at every fixed density.
No lower bound on all algorithms is inferred from this failure.

\section{Audit}
The original discussion on printed page 1531 was inspected. The audit
keeps approximation of a number separate from producing an assignment,
and expectation ratios separate from expected ratios or high-probability
claims. Clauses with repeated variables are permitted in the explicitly
analyzed model, so no false pointwise $7m/8$ guarantee is used.
No random-instance experiment or current-literature completeness claim
was made. The density dependence leaves the original all-accuracy,
fixed-density target unresolved.
